title: Whitehead theorem for spaces of CW homotopy type
statement: Use the path components and continuous based homotopy groups of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. A CW complex here is a space formed from the empty space by attaching, for each $n\geq0$, a set of closed $n$-disks along their boundary spheres to the $(n-1)$-skeleton, with the weak topology for the characteristic disk maps and with the boundary of each cell contained in finitely many lower-dimensional cells. The empty space is allowed. A homotopy equivalence is a continuous map $u:A\to B$ admitting a continuous $r:B\to A$ with $ru\simeq\operatorname{id}_A$ and $ur\simeq\operatorname{id}_B$, where homotopies use ordinary product with $[0,1]$ and need not fix basepoints. Let $X,Y$ be topological spaces each homotopy equivalent to a CW complex. If a continuous map $f:X\to Y$ induces a bijection on path components and an isomorphism $\pi_n(X,x)\to\pi_n(Y,f(x))$ for every $x\in X$ and integer $n\geq1$, then $f$ is a homotopy equivalence. No connectedness or nonemptiness hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Proposition 3.6.3.8 (Tag 013X), Whitehead theorem; CW meaning as in Remark 1.2.3.12 Read online 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/. Kerodon tag, not a Stacks tag; no Stacks tag for this comparison theorem was found.

proof.text: If $X=\varnothing$, surjectivity on path components forces $Y=\varnothing$: any point of $Y$ would give a component. If $Y=\varnothing$, the existence of $f$ forces $X=\varnothing$. In either case the unique maps are inverse. Otherwise unpack the CW-homotopy-type hypothesis on $Y$: take a CW complex $C$, maps $u:C\to Y$ and $v:Y\to C$, and homotopies $uv\simeq\operatorname{id}_Y$, $vu\simeq\operatorname{id}_C$. All homotopies below use ordinary interval products.

source.place: Proposition 3.6.3.8, choice of a CW model for the target and empty cases

proof.text: Apply [lem-cbc-cw-source-homotopy-lift] to $w=f:X\to Y$ and $u:C\to Y$. Its weak-equivalence hypotheses are precisely those assumed on $f$, and $C$ is CW. Obtain $a:C\to X$ and $fa\simeq u$. Set $g=av:Y\to X$. Composing the supplied homotopy with $v$ gives $fg=fav\simeq uv\simeq\operatorname{id}_Y$. Thus $g$ is a right homotopy inverse, with no claim yet about $gf$.

source.place: Proposition 3.6.3.8, first application of Lemma 3.6.3.11 and construction of a right inverse

proof.text: The self-map $fg:Y\to Y$ is a homotopy equivalence with inverse $\operatorname{id}_Y$: each of its two composites with that map is $fg$, and the homotopy of step 2 joins it to $\operatorname{id}_Y$. Apply [lem-coef-homotopy-equivalence-weak] to this self-map and this inverse. It gives a component bijection and isomorphisms on every positive homotopy group at every source point for $fg$, even though the given homotopy can move the point. On components $(fg)_*=f_*g_*$ and both $(fg)_*$ and $f_*$ are bijections, so $g_*=f_*^{-1}(fg)_*$ is a bijection. Postcomposition sends paths to paths, so on components composition of maps induces composition of functions. For a cubical representative $q:([0,1]^n,\partial[0,1]^n)\to(Y,y)$, postcomposition sends its class to the class of $g\circ q$, and then to the class of $f\circ g\circ q$; postcomposition also preserves relative-boundary homotopies and concatenation in the first coordinate. Thus these induced maps are homomorphisms and, for every $y\in Y$ and $n\geq1$, $(fg)_{*,y}=f_{*,g(y)}\circ g_{*,y}$. Here $f_{*,g(y)}$ is an isomorphism by hypothesis, so $g_{*,y}=f_{*,g(y)}^{-1}\circ(fg)_{*,y}$ is an isomorphism. Thus $g$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. This cancellation is between maps ending in $\pi_n(Y,fg(y))$; it never identifies that group with $\pi_n(Y,y)$ by an identity map.

source.place: Proposition 3.6.3.8, weak equivalence of the right inverse, with the component and based-group cancellation expanded

proof.text: Unpack the CW-homotopy-type hypothesis on $X$: choose a CW complex $D$, maps $b:D\to X$ and $c:X\to D$, and a homotopy $bc\simeq\operatorname{id}_X$. Apply [lem-cbc-cw-source-homotopy-lift] to the weak equivalence $g:Y\to X$ proved in step 3 and the map $b$. This gives $d:D\to Y$ with $gd\simeq b$. Set $h=dc:X\to Y$; then $gh=gdc\simeq bc\simeq\operatorname{id}_X$. The CW source is $D$; the two other spaces need not carry chosen CW structures.

source.place: Proposition 3.6.3.8, second application of Lemma 3.6.3.11, to the right inverse

proof.text: Compose the homotopy $gh\simeq\operatorname{id}_X$ on the left with $gf$, reversing it, and compose $fg\simeq\operatorname{id}_Y$ on the left with $g$ and on the right with $h$. These give $gf\simeq gfgh=g(fg)h\simeq gh\simeq\operatorname{id}_X$. Together with step 2, $fg\simeq\operatorname{id}_Y$, this proves that $g$ is a two-sided homotopy inverse for the given $f$. Composition preserves continuity of homotopies; concatenate any two by using the first on $0\leq t\leq1/2$ with parameter $2t$ and the second on $1/2\leq t\leq1$ with parameter $2t-1$. The endpoint maps coincide at $1/2$, so the pasting is continuous. No based homotopy or triangle-compatible choice is required.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 3.6.3.8, read online 2026-10-17; its two CW-source lifting applications followed, with moving-basepoint cancellation and explicit homotopy pasting expanded. Not archived in literature/; WANTED in report.
